stops.narrative: Inspect the signs and numerical impressions. Keep the probable grain interpretation separate from a complete translation.
Find scenes of offerings and music. Ask why an elite funerary wall selected these activities.
Locate the arid island setting. Compare what reservoirs reveal with what the seal’s unread signs cannot yet tell us.
Inspect the jade’s geometry and then think about waterworks and burials. Do not give a city, culture and artifact one artificial lifespan.
Imagine questions you could ask of platforms and sunken courts. The comparison with Liangzhu implies no historical contact.
Consider hearths, beds and a tool of uncertain use. Explain which evidence supports a conclusion and what may be missing.

conclusion: Early communities become visible through many kinds of evidence. Records, monuments and surviving houses illuminate different people and activities. A serious atlas can compare them without ranking their worth or pretending they share one political lineage.

evidence.prompt: Which statement makes the strongest supported distinction?

options.text: Every ancient sign can be translated if we imagine what its maker wanted.
options.feedback: Imagination is not a translation method. The Indus signs remain incompletely read, while even the grain tablet’s interpretation has limits.

options.text: A building, a tablet and a burial object can support different questions about a society.
options.feedback: Their materials, contexts and purposes preserve different information. Compare the questions each can answer.

options.text: Monumental buildings prove that everyone in a community had equal power.
options.feedback: Coordinated work does not establish equality. Differentiated spaces and burials may instead prompt questions about hierarchy.
